source.title: Do Language Models Encode Knowledge of Linguistic Constraint Violations?

record.tranche_reason: The paper motivates using SAEs by saying model activations are often polysemantic and entangled, but its experiments test candidate grammatical-violation features, not whether neurons respond to unrelated inputs.
record.gate_note: The study ablates SAE features selected for preferential activation on grammatical violations and measures effects on sentence likelihood. Those outcomes concern grammaticality-detector selectivity, not the unrelated-input responses named by the claim versions. Table 1 reports per-model counts of phenomena passing the criteria; its broad pattern is recorded under fits_no_version. The paper also reports BLiMP accuracy, but that is a task-performance result rather than a measurement of polysemanticity.
record.test_reason: The paper cites polysemantic, entangled activations (Elhage 2022; Bricken 2023) only to motivate using pretrained SAEs. Its experiments ablate SAE features selected for grammatical-violation sensitivity and score effects on sentence likelihood. It never measures how often neurons respond to unrelated inputs, or what causes or changes that.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors find limited support for dedicated grammatical-violation detector features: the three criteria are rarely met jointly, and no features are shared across all phenomena. Violation-related information is not cleanly separable from general sentence-level representations.
record.recipe_differences: Uses SAE sensitivity scores to select candidate grammatical-violation features and tests them with activation ablation against random-feature controls; unlike the original vision-neuron examples and SoLU work, it does not measure polysemanticity rates or test the original procedures.
record.method_sensitivity: Layer selection and top-k selection matter: Table 2 uses a revised layer-selection rule compared with Table 1, producing different aggregate counts. The authors also report that F2 remains largely unfulfilled in the top-1 setting.

fits_no_version.finding: SAE features with high violation sensitivity also causally shift the likelihood of well-formed sentences. F1 passes broadly, but F2 rarely passes, even with top-1 features (Table 1, Sec. 4.2). The authors call this an intrinsic entanglement and link it to SAE feature absorption.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features in language models that are selectively more active on grammatical violations are not causally specific to violations; ablating them also affects general sentence likelihood.

record.problems: The authors state that computational constraints limited the range of model sizes and that their falsification tests do not cover all relevant linguistic phenomena. Results depend on their sensitivity score, SAE features, and ablation framework. The text gives significance thresholds and pass counts but not confidence intervals or effect-size uncertainty.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2's per-phenomenon GPT-2 measurements are not recorded as additional rows: they test the same grammatical-violation detector criteria rather than unrelated-input responses or polysemanticity as defined in the claim versions.

untested.parts: No measurement of MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts, or of their share by layer.
No test of superposition as the cause of polysemanticity.
No test of initialization, regularization or training noise as causes.
No comparison of polysemanticity rates across activation functions, architectures or regularization. The SAE architectures differ across model families, but that is incidental.
No reanalysis of canonical polysemantic neurons.
No test of how activation range or explanation scoring changes polysemanticity labels.

record.verdict_notes: Polysemanticity appears only as a cited motivation for using SAEs. The paper counts six models, although the methods text says five Transformer models; Table 1 shows six (GPT-2, Gemma-3 270M/1B/4B, Qwen3.5 2B/9B).

versions.untested_parts: No image classifier or vision neuron is studied.
The study does not measure MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts, or the share of such neurons.
It does not test whether feature superposition results from representing more features than available neurons.
It does not test initialization, regularization, or training noise as causes of polysemanticity.

Although it uses different SAE architectures across model families, it does not compare polysemanticity rates across activations, architectures, or regularization, or measure a performance trade-off from reducing such rates.
It does not investigate whether canonical polysemantic neurons detect a shared feature or related offshoots of one job.
Its layer and top-k choices concern grammatical-violation feature tests; it does not test how the measured prevalence of polysemantic neurons changes with activation range or explanation scoring.

rows.subject: GPT-2 (240M)
rows.operation_detail: Ablated top-k SAE candidate features selected by their sensitivity to grammatical violations; compared with random-feature ablation.
rows.measure: Number of phenomena passing each ablation criterion, reported as F1/F2/F3; F1∩F2/F2∩F3/F1∩F3; F1∩F2∩F3
rows.baseline: Equal-sized random feature ablation for the criterion comparisons
rows.note: The methods section calls GPT-2 small 124M, while Table 1 labels this result GPT-2 (240M). Counts are phenomena passing criteria, not counts of polysemantic neurons.
rows.check: Table 1 labels the model GPT-2 (240M), but the methods section says GPT-2 small (124M). The value counts BLiMP phenomena passing the falsification criteria, not polysemantic neurons. It is SAE-feature ablation, not a polysemanticity measure.
